1:1: This is a common expression of this culture that means that the Lord spoke a message to Joel.
1:2: שִׁמְעוּ־זֹאת הַזְּקֵנִים וְהַאֲזִינוּ כֹּל יוֹשְׁבֵי הָאָרֶץ
See the discussion in the introduction to Joel of how Hebrew poetry consisted of paired phrases that meant basically the same thing.
הֶהָיְתָה זֹּאת בִּימֵיכֶם וְאִם בִּימֵי אֲבֹתֵיכֶם
Joel is using the question form for emphasis.
Joel is using the term days to mean a period of time by association with the way days make up longer periods of time.
Joel is not referring to the literal fathers of the Israelites whom he is addressing. He is using that term to mean their ancestors.
1:4: The terms cutting, swarming, hopping, and destroying describe different kinds of locusts. Interpreters are not certain specifically what kinds of locusts these were.
1:5: This is an expression that means that something is no longer available.
1:6: See the discussion in the introduction to Joel of travel descriptions marked for change in elevation.
Joel is making an overstatement for emphasis.
שִׁנָּיו שִׁנֵּי אַרְיֵה וּמְתַלְּעוֹת לָבִיא לוֹ
Joel is describing the locusts as if they literally had the teeth of lions and lionesses. He means that they have strong teeth that can chew even the toughest of plants.
שִׁנָּיו שִׁנֵּי אַרְיֵה וּמְתַלְּעוֹת לָבִיא לוֹ
These two phrases, Its teeth {are} the teeth of a lion, and the fangs of a lioness {are} to it, mean similar things. Joel is using repetition to emphasize the idea that the phrases express.
1:7: Joel is speaking as if the locusts had literally thrown … away the vegetation they had finished eating.
Joel is using the term have become white to mean that the branches have been stripped of their bark, by association with the way the wood underneath the bark is white in color.
1:8: The point of this comparison is that just as a virgin dresses in sackcloth to express her grief, so the Israelites should mourn to express their grief.
To wear sackcloth, which is clothing made of rough, uncomfortable fabric, is a symbolic action that expresses grief.

Joel assumes that his listeners will know that by the husband of her youth, he means the fiancé to whom a young woman was betrothed. The word virgin indicates that this woman was not yet married, but in this culture, engagement was tantamount to marriage and a fiancé was considered a husband.
1:9: The phrase have been cut off is an expression that means that something is no longer available.
As the introduction to this chapter discusses, here and often in this chapter, Joel is using the word house to mean “temple.”
1:10: Joel is speaking of the ground as if it were a living thing that could mourn because it was bare of crops.
Joel is speaking as if the new wine the Israelites would have gotten from this harvest had literally dried up.
Here Joel is speaking of the supply of oil as if it had been strong and now was weak.
1:12: Here Joel is speaking of the fig tree as if it had been strong and now was weak.
Joel is making an overstatement for emphasis.
Joel is speaking of joy as if it were a liquid that had literally dried up.
1:13: To lodge in sackcloth is a symbolic action that expresses deep mourning and repentance.
1:14: A fast is a time of going without eating. In this context, not eating would be a symbolic action to express sorrow for the sins that had caused the Lord to punish the Israelites.
1:15: Joel is using the term day to mean “this particular time of trouble,” by association with the way a day is a specific period of time.
Joel is using the term day to mean the time when the Lord will judge and punish his enemies, by association with the way days make up specific periods of time.
The word Shaddai is another name for God.
1:16: Joel is using the question form for emphasis.
Joel is using the term eyes to mean sight, by association with the way eyes are used for seeing.
The terms joy and gladness mean similar things. Joel is using the two terms together for emphasis.
1:17: Joel is speaking of grain as if it were a liquid that had dried up.
1:18: Joel is speaking of the sheep dying from hunger as if they were literally being punished.
1:19: Joel is speaking of the locusts’ destruction as if it were literally a fire consuming the pastures.
Joel is speaking of the locusts’ destruction as if it were literally a flame burning the trees.
2:1: תִּקְעוּ שׁוֹפָר בְּצִיּוֹן וְהָרִיעוּ בְּהַר קָדְשִׁי
Joel assumes that his listeners will know that he wants them to do the things he describes in order to sound an alarm.
A shofar is a trumpet made from a ram’s horn.
Joel assumes that his listeners will know that by tremble he means to tremble in fear or awe.
2:2: יוֹם חֹשֶׁךְ וַאֲפֵלָה יוֹם עָנָן וַעֲרָפֶל
Joel is using the term day to mean a period of time, by association with the way days make up specific periods of time.
The terms darkness and gloom mean similar things. Joel is using the two terms together for emphasis.
The terms clouds and thick darkness mean similar things. Joel is using the two terms together for emphasis.
The point of this comparison is that just as the dawn spreads in a steady and unstoppable way across the mountains, so the army of locusts spreads in the same way across the land.
Joel is using the term dawn by association to mean the light that appears at dawn.
The terms great and mighty mean similar things. Joel is using the two terms together for emphasis.
Joel is making an overstatement for emphasis.
2:3: לְפָנָיו אָכְלָה אֵשׁ וְאַחֲרָיו תְּלַהֵט לֶהָבָה
Joel is speaking of the locusts’ destruction as if it were literally a fire consuming everything in front of it and leaving burning land behind.
See the discussion in the introduction to this chapter of how several phrases with the word face mean “in front of.”
The point of this comparison is that just as the garden of Eden was very lush, so the land of Israel ahead of the locust invasion is lush.
Joel is making an overstatement for emphasis.
2:4: The point of this comparison is that just like war horses, the locusts appear to be strong and fearless.
The point of this comparison is that just as galloping steeds travel very quickly and seem to be flying as they are running, so the locusts travels quickly as it flies.
2:5: The point of this comparison is that just as chariots make a loud, rumbling noise, so the locusts make a loud noise as they move across the land.
The point of this comparison is that just as a fire makes a crackling sound as it quickly consumes dry stubble, so the locusts make a similar sound as they quickly consume the vegetation.
The point of this comparison is that just as a mighty army gives a loud shout once it is arrayed for war, so the locusts are making a loud and terrifying noise.
2:6: Joel assumes that his listeners will know that by writhe he means to writhe in agony or fear.
Joel is using the term beauty to mean paleness by association with the way pale skin was considered beautiful in that culture.
2:7: The point of this comparison is that the locusts rush forward irresistibly, just as warriors do.
The point of this comparison is that just as men of war skillfully scale walls in battle, so the locusts surmount obstacles without difficulty.
In this context, man means “each one” and ways refers to the ways that a locust is traveling.
Joel is speaking of the locusts staying on their paths as if those paths were literally something they could give in pledge.
See the discussion in the introduction to this chapter of an alternate reading for this phrase.
2:8: Here, man means “each one” and brother means “another one.” This expression describes how the locusts move in an orderly manner.
As in the previous clause, man means “each one” and road refers to the direction of travel.
2:9: The point of this comparison is that just as thieves enter unexpectedly and undetected through windows, so the locusts get into homes in ways that people do not anticipate and so, cannot prevent.
2:10: Joel is speaking as if the locust swarm were so powerful that it was causing the earth to shake and the heavens to tremble. He means that the locusts make such a loud sound and cause such vibration that it seems like this is happening.
Joel is speaking as if the sun and the moon had literally become dark. He means that the locust swarm is blocking their light.
Joel is speaking of the stars as if they were living things that could withdraw their brightness.
2:11: Joel is using the term voice to mean the Lord’s commands, by association with the way authorities use their voices to give commands.
Joel is using the term camp to mean the Lord’s army, by association with the way armies stay in camps.
Joel is using the term word to mean the Lord’s orders, by association with the way people use words to give orders or instructions.
כִּי־גָדוֹל יוֹם־יְהוָה וְנוֹרָא מְאֹד וּמִי יְכִילֶנּוּ
Joel is using the question form for emphasis.
2:12: Here, the Lord is speaking of people repenting of their sin as a return to him, and he is speaking of their heart to represent their thoughts and motives.
2:13: Joel is speaking as if people could literally tear their hearts. He is using the contrast with tearing garments, which was a literal sign of mourning, to emphasize internal repentance.
Here, long of nostrils is an idiom meaning that the person is slow to get angry.
2:14: מִי יוֹדֵעַ יָשׁוּב וְנִחָם וְהִשְׁאִיר אַחֲרָיו בְּרָכָה
Joel is using the question form for emphasis.
The terms turn and relent mean similar things. Joel is using the two terms together for emphasis.
2:15: Joel assumes that his readers will understand that the purpose of a fast was to show repentance for sin.
2:16: קִבְצוּ זְקֵנִים אִסְפוּ עוֹלָלִים וְיֹנְקֵי שָׁדָיִם
Joel is speaking of two things in order to mean those two extremes and everything in between.
Joel means implicitly that while newlyweds are ordinarily excused from public duties, this is an exceptional circumstance that calls for even their attendance.
2:17: Joel is speaking of these two things that are at the far extremes of the courtyard of the temple in order to refer to them and to everything in between them.
Joel is speaking of the Israelites as if they were literally something that the Lord had inherited. Joel means that the Israelites are the people whom the Lord has chosen.
See the discussion in the introduction to this chapter of an alternate reading for this phrase.
Joel is using the question form for emphasis.
This example of mockery is also using the question form for emphasis.
2:18: Joel is using the term land by association to mean the people living on the land.
2:19: This phrase expresses a single idea by using two words connected with and. The word answered tells for what purpose the Lord said this.
The expression Behold me doing something means “I am going to do” what is described.
2:20: The Lord is using the term northerner to refer to an invading army of some kind, by association with the direction from which invasions often came. It seems that this term is purposely vague so that it can refer to the current locust invasion as well as to a future military invasion on “the day of the Lord” (verse 11). If possible, use a term that could refer to both.
The terms dryness and desolation mean similar things. The Lord is using the two terms together for emphasis.
אֶל … אֶת־פָּנָיו אֶל־הַיָּם הַקַּדְמֹנִי וְסֹפוֹ אֶל־הַיָּם הָאַחֲרוֹן
The Lord is speaking of the invading army or locust swarm as if it were a living thing that had a face and a back.
אֶל … אֶת־פָּנָיו אֶל־הַיָּם הַקַּדְמֹנִי וְסֹפוֹ אֶל־הַיָּם הָאַחֲרוֹן
The Lord is speaking to the Judeans from the perspective of their own culture and location. By eastern sea, he means the Dead Sea, and by western sea, he means the Mediterranean Sea.
These two phrases mean the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words.

This expression means “he has in some way done more than would be expected.” The implication is that the locust swarm has perhaps destroyed more crops than it ordinarily would, or that the army that will invade will be more destructive than usual.
2:21: Joel is speaking to the land as if it were a person who could hear him. He is doing this to show in a strong way how he feels about what the Lord will do for the land. Joel is actually speaking to the people who can hear him.
The terms glad and rejoice mean similar things. Joel is using the two terms together for emphasis.
2:22: Joel is once again speaking to the beasts of the field as if they were people who could hear him. He is doing this to show his Judean listeners in a strong way how he feels about what the Lord will do for them by restoring the pastures and the trees.
Joel is using the term strength to mean the harvest, by association with the way the land has the capacity to produce crops.
2:23: Joel is speaking as if Zion, meaning Jerusalem, were literally the mother of the people who lived in that city.
Joel is speaking from the perspective of his own culture and location. By early rain he means the fall rains, and by late rain he means the spring rains.
Joel is speaking from the perspective of his own culture. By in the first, he could mean either (1) or (2)
2:24: Joel is making an overstatement for emphasis.
2:25: The Lord is using the term years by association to mean the crops produced in those years.
The Lord is speaking of the locust swarm as if it were literally his army.
2:26: The Lord is using the term name to mean character or reputation, by association with the way a name represents a person’s identity.
The word translated as forever means “to indefinite futurity.”
2:27: While it is not known precisely where or when Joel prophesied, he appears to have lived in the southern kingdom of Judah before the exile or in the province of Judah (Judea) after the exile. So the term Israel probably does not mean the northern kingdom of Israel. It seems to be a reference to the people of Judah as Israelites.
The word translated as forever means “to indefinite futurity.”
2:28: The Lord is speaking as if he would literally pour out his Spirit like a liquid. He means that he will give his Spirit generously.
The Lord is using the term flesh to mean people, by association with the way human bodies are made of flesh.
The Lord says all here as a generalization for emphasis.
The Lord is speaking of the two major components of something in order to mean everything it includes.
זִקְנֵיכֶם חֲלֹמוֹת יַחֲלֹמוּן בַּחוּרֵיכֶם חֶזְיֹנוֹת יִרְאוּ
The Lord is speaking of two things in order to refer to them and everything in between.
Joel assumes that his listeners will know that by dreams he means dreams with prophetic significance.
2:29: The Lord is speaking of two things in order to mean them and everything in between. This verse continues the thought of the previous verse, that the Spirit will come to a great variety of people.
The Lord is using the term days to mean a period of time, by association with the way days make up longer periods of time.
2:31: The Lord is speaking as if the sun and moon would literally turn into darkness and blood. He means that they will appear as they do during eclipses.
2:32: The Lord is using one aspect of the Lord, his name, to represent all of the Lord.
The terms Mount Zion and Jerusalem mean similar things. The Lord is using the two terms together for emphasis.
3:1: The Lord is using the term behold to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say.
The expressions in those days and at that time mean similar things. The Lord is using the two expressions together for emphasis.
See the discussion in the introduction to this chapter of an alternate reading for this phrase.
3:2: The word Jehoshaphat is the name of a valley.

This phrase expresses a single idea by using two words connected with and. The word inheritance tells what kind of people the Israelites are to the Lord. In this context, the word inheritance refers to a portion that someone would choose for himself.
3:4: The Lord is using the question form for emphasis.
This is an expression that a person in this culture would commonly use to ask another person why he was treating him with hostility.
הַגְּמוּל אַתֶּם מְשַׁלְּמִים עָלָי וְאִם־גֹּמְלִים אַתֶּם עָלַי
The Lord is speaking as if the nations were literally paying him back for something bad that he had done to them. He is asking if they have a grudge against him that they are carrying out.
The terms swiftly and speedily mean similar things. The Lord is using the two terms together for emphasis.
The Lord is using one part of a person, his head, to mean the entire person.
3:6: Here the word sons does not mean literal first-generation offspring but “descendants.” The phrase the sons of Javan refers to the Ionians, that is, the Greeks.
3:8: וּמָכַרְתִּי אֶת־בְּנֵיכֶם וְאֶת־בְּנוֹתֵיכֶם בְּיַד בְּנֵי יְהוּדָה
The Lord is using one part of a person, the hand, to represent the whole person in the act of taking possession of something.
Here the word sons does not mean literal first-generation offspring but “descendants.” The phrase the sons of Judah refers to the Judeans.
The word Sabeans is the name of a people group.
3:9: Joel assumes that his listeners will know that by Consecrate a war he means to perform the rites with which they would begin a war.
3:10: The word plowshares describes blades for plows, which are tools used to break up soil for planting.
The expression pruning hooks describes curved blades used for trimming trees and vines.
3:11: This phrase expresses a single idea by using two words connected with and. The word Hurry tells in what way the nations should come.
3:12: To sit to judge means to sit down as a symbolic action that represents taking an official position of authority to make judgments.
3:13: שִׁלְחוּ מַגָּל כִּי בָשַׁל קָצִיר … כִּי
The Lord is speaking as if he literally wanted the “warriors” mentioned in 3:11 to harvest grain. He means that he wants them to punish the nations.
The Lord is using the first action that someone would do in order to use a sickle, Stretch it out, to refer to the entire act of using it.
The Lord is speaking as if he literally wanted those “warriors” to press grapes. He means once again that he wants them to punish the nations.
3:15: שֶׁמֶשׁ וְיָרֵחַ קָדָרוּ וְכוֹכָבִים אָסְפוּ נָגְהָם

These are the same phrases as in 2:10, where Joel used them to describe the locust swarm blocking the light of the sun, moon, and stars. Here, in Joel’s description of the final judgment, these phrases could: (1) have a literal meaning, describing how the creation will disintegrate at the end of history. Or; (2) be symbolic of earthly rulers and nations losing their power.
3:16: Joel is speaking as if the Lord would literally roar like a lion. He means that the Lord will powerfully proclaim his judgments.

Joel is speaking as if the heavens and the earth would literally shake. This could be: (1) a literal description of how the creation will disintegrate at the end of history. Or; (2) a symbolic description of how powers on earth and in heaven will give way before the power of the Lord.
וַיהוָה מַחֲסֶה לְעַמּוֹ וּמָעוֹז לִבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל
Joel is describing the Lord as a shelter and a stronghold. He means that the Lord will protect his people.
3:18: The Lord is using the term day to mean a specific time, by association with the way a day is a specific period of time.
יִטְּפוּ הֶהָרִים עָסִיס וְהַגְּבָעוֹת תֵּלַכְנָה חָלָב
The Lord is describing the mountains and hills as producing wine and milk. He means that the land will be very productive.
The Lord is using the term spring by association to mean the water that comes from a spring.
The word Shittim is the name of a valley.
3:19: The Lord is using the term blood to mean the lives of people, by association with the way people’s blood may be shed when they are killed.
3:20: The Lord is using the term Judah by association to mean the people living in Judah.
3:21: See the discussion in the introduction to this chapter of an alternate reading for this phrase.
The Lord is using the term blood to mean the deaths of people, by association with the loss of blood that usually occurs when people die violently.
